power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .908", "p = .051", "p = .070", "p = .174", "p = .855"), Sentence = c("Δr = -.094 (p = .022), -.085 (p = .015), +.040 (p = .908); combined Z = 1.636, p = .051.", "Δr = -.094 (p = .022), -.085 (p = .015), +.040 (p = .908); combined Z = 1.636, p = .051.", "Study 2 replication at 3B: Δr = -.082 (p = .070); self-agreement .701.", "Combined Z = 0.939, one-tailed p = .174; not supported.", "Across the nine models the slope of Fisher z on log₁₀ active parameters was 0.009 (SE = 0.048, p = .855), against 0.255 under the controlled software setup." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2361 columns across 208 data files.
#### Issues Identified

10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

102 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **102 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 208 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Passing the Wrong Test: Model Size and Discriminant Validity in LLM-Based Psychological Assessment

text.text: Validation studies of zero-shot language-model scoring of psychological interviews often rely primarily on a single convergent correlation with a questionnaire to establish validity.
However, a bivariate correlation cannot reveal whether a model lacks discriminant validity, agrees poorly in absolute terms, produces non-random missing scores, or scores inconsistently.
We evaluated eight open-weight families (1-70B active parameters) and eight commercial frontier models.
The models scored the same sets of clinical interviews (Study 1: suicide recovery, 𝑛 = 149; Study 2: future self-continuity, 𝑛 = 164) across 52 configurations.
Convergent validity improves with model size in both studies.

However, the standard open-weight models tested achieve only about three-quarters of frontier convergent validity, with 11-fold greater mean absolute bias, more format failures, and lower repeatability in Study 1.

In Study 2, standard open models (≤ 27B) are as strongly correlated with a closely related construct (suicide recovery) as with the target (mean difference -0.014), although they correlate less strongly with a distal neighbor (life satisfaction).
All six frontier generations correlate more strongly with the target than with either neighbor (mean difference from recovery +0.117).
On a local workstation, Gemma 4 31B is within the frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, outperforming its similar-sized predecessor.
Llama 3.3 70B shows no greater discriminant validity than Gemma 4 31B, suggesting that discriminant validity is a function of release, not parameter count alone.
Based on these findings, we suggest a minimum validation standard across five domains.
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have made it possible to automatically score open-ended psychological interviews.

Specifically, a model can take a verbatim transcript of an interview and a set of natural-language instructions describing how to score the interview, without any training examples (i.e., zero-shot), and output a numerical rating of a psychological construct.

LLM ratings of interviews and other open-ended text have been shown to correlate with validated measures of personality (Wright et al., 2026), life satisfaction (Mesquiti et al., 2026), spirituality (Prinzing et al., 2025), depression (Ohse et al., 2024), and clinician-rated symptom severity in people at clinical high risk for psychosis (Chen et al., 2026; but see Teferra et al., 2026, for posttraumatic stress symptoms; for discussion, see Abdurahman et al., 2024; Demszky et al., 2023).
text.formatted: LLM ratings of interviews and other open-ended text have been shown to correlate with validated measures of personality <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Wright et al., 2026)</ref>, life satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mesquiti et al., 2026)</ref>, spirituality <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Prinzing et al., 2025)</ref>, depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ohse et al., 2024)</ref>, and clinician-rated symptom severity in people at clinical high risk for psychosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chen et al., 2026</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Teferra et al., 2026</ref>, for posttraumatic stress symptoms; for discussion, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abdurahman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Demszky et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This method differs from previous word-list and supervised methods (Pennebaker et al., 2015) in that it only requires the rubric used by human raters, not any training examples (Ziems et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This method differs from previous word-list and supervised methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Pennebaker et al., 2015)</ref> in that it only requires the rubric used by human raters, not any training examples <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Ziems et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This method has been applied to psychotherapy sessions (Eberhardt et al., 2025) and to psychiatric interviews, with a few scored examples added to the prompt (Girard et al., 2026), and in suicide research to create measures of future self-continuity (FSC; Sokol & Goodman, 2026) and recovery after a suicidal episode (Sokol et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This method has been applied to psychotherapy sessions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Eberhardt et al., 2025)</ref> and to psychiatric interviews, with a few scored examples added to the prompt <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Girard et al., 2026)</ref>, and in suicide research to create measures of future self-continuity (FSC; <ref type="bibr">Sokol & Goodman, 2026)</ref> and recovery after a suicidal episode <ref type="bibr">(Sokol et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In most cases, validity evidence consists of a single statistic: a convergent correlation between the model's score and a source questionnaire, or agreement with a human rating (Törnberg, 2024).
text.formatted: In most cases, validity evidence consists of a single statistic: a convergent correlation between the model's score and a source questionnaire, or agreement with a human rating <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Törnberg, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: When researchers compare different models, they typically rank them based on this statistic, assuming that the model with the higher correlation is the better measure (Girard et al., 2026).
text.formatted: When researchers compare different models, they typically rank them based on this statistic, assuming that the model with the higher correlation is the better measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Girard et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Some studies have also reported internal consistency, factor structure, or correlations with outcomes (Eberhardt et al., 2025; Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Some studies have also reported internal consistency, factor structure, or correlations with outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Eberhardt et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Others have labeled multiple constructs within the same design (Ziems et al., 2024) or examined discriminant validity with supervised language models (Gu et al., 2026; Oltmanns et al., 2026). Low et al. (2026) recently proposed a broader framework for evaluating the psychometric properties of textderived psychological measures, including content validity, construct validity, and reliability.
text.formatted: Others have labeled multiple constructs within the same design <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Ziems et al., 2024)</ref> or examined discriminant validity with supervised language models <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Oltmanns et al., 2026)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Low et al. (2026)</ref> recently proposed a broader framework for evaluating the psychometric properties of textderived psychological measures, including content validity, construct validity, and reliability.

text.text: They showed that methods with good criterion validity can still miss prototypical expressions of the intended construct, so a single performance statistic can hide important measurement problems.

However, we found no psychological measure, scored zero-shot by an LLM, that has been evaluated with a formal discriminant comparison against a neighboring questionnaire or a check of first-attempt scoring failures, and few that have been evaluated for limits of agreement or repeatability (Pimentel & Meyer, 2026; Sokol & Goodman, 2026).
text.formatted: However, we found no psychological measure, scored zero-shot by an LLM, that has been evaluated with a formal discriminant comparison against a neighboring questionnaire or a check of first-attempt scoring failures, and few that have been evaluated for limits of agreement or repeatability <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Pimentel & Meyer, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sokol & Goodman, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A single correlation has never been sufficient evidence of validity (Loevinger, 1957; Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994).
text.formatted: A single correlation has never been sufficient evidence of validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Loevinger, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Construct validity requires that a measure of a construct not only correlate with measures of the same construct (convergent validity), but also be distinguishable from measures of neighboring constructs (discriminant validity; Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Messick, 1995).
text.formatted: Construct validity requires that a measure of a construct not only correlate with measures of the same construct (convergent validity), but also be distinguishable from measures of neighboring constructs <ref type="bibr">(discriminant validity;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cronbach & Meehl, 1955;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Messick, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The discriminant requirement is a routine part of questionnaire validation (Clark & Watson, 2019), but is seldom applied to model-derived scores.
text.formatted: The discriminant requirement is a routine part of questionnaire validation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Clark & Watson, 2019)</ref>, but is seldom applied to model-derived scores.

text.text: For example, in the field of automated text analysis, researchers have used the presence of firstperson singular pronouns ("I-talk") as an indicator of depression, based on bivariate associations between the two variables.
Only recently have discriminant tests been run, indicating that "I-talk" is a marker of general negative emotionality, not just depression (Tackman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Only recently have discriminant tests been run, indicating that "I-talk" is a marker of general negative emotionality, not just depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Tackman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A convergent correlation does not tell us anything about these four properties.

First, poor discriminant validity: A model instructed to score Construct A may nonetheless produce scores that correlate just as strongly with Construct B, either because the model fails to distinguish the intended construct from a neighboring one or because its scores reflect a broader feature of the participant or the interview (e.g., general distress, narrative coherence, interview length).
Second, poor absolute agreement: A model may produce scores that correlate strongly with a self-report scale, but each score differs from the self-report scale by a scale point.
While the strength of association is unchanged (Pearson's 𝑟), the model's scores cannot be interpreted in terms of the cutoffs of the scale.
Third, non-random missing scores: When a model fails to produce a usable score, the case is typically excluded from analysis.
If these failures are not random, however, they effectively determine the analytic sample (Rubin, 1976).
text.formatted: If these failures are not random, however, they effectively determine the analytic sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Rubin, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, poor repeatability: Because models produce responses stochastically, a smaller model's lower validity may be due to its own response variability just as much as to less accurate scoring.
Only repeated independent scoring passes can distinguish between these two possibilities.

The lack of attention to such properties has had consequences in suicide research, where, for many years, published summary statistics failed to indicate how poorly prediction models performed in practice (Belsher et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The lack of attention to such properties has had consequences in suicide research, where, for many years, published summary statistics failed to indicate how poorly prediction models performed in practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Belsher et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers with sensitive transcripts face a second challenge.

Outsource scoring to a commercial provider and researchers risk violating confidentiality and data agreements, as well as institutional data security and review requirements (European Union, 2016; Marks & Haupt, 2023).
text.formatted: Outsource scoring to a commercial provider and researchers risk violating confidentiality and data agreements, as well as institutional data security and review requirements <ref type="bibr">(European Union, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Marks & Haupt, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In response to these and other concerns, researchers have expressed a desire for openweight models that they can run on their own machines (Girard et al., 2026; Palmer et al., 2024; Riedemann et al., 2024; Wiest et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In response to these and other concerns, researchers have expressed a desire for openweight models that they can run on their own machines <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Girard et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Palmer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Riedemann et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Wiest et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to the ethical considerations, open-weight models are also more cost-effective per transcript.

However, there is a lack of evidence to guide researchers in selecting the best local model. Brickman et al.'s (2025) recently published methodological guide for LLM-based psychological assessment lists criteria for model selection but offers no evidence on how to choose among models.
text.formatted: However, there is a lack of evidence to guide researchers in selecting the best local model. <ref type="bibr">Brickman et al.'s (2025)</ref> recently published methodological guide for LLM-based psychological assessment lists criteria for model selection but offers no evidence on how to choose among models.

text.text: In studies that compare multiple models, researchers have varied the prompt, sampling settings, or the platform used to run each model, in addition to the model itself (e.g., Alizadeh et al., 2025), so the model's own contribution cannot be isolated.
text.formatted: In studies that compare multiple models, researchers have varied the prompt, sampling settings, or the platform used to run each model, in addition to the model itself (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Alizadeh et al., 2025)</ref>, so the model's own contribution cannot be isolated.

text.text: Other studies have shown that performance on text classification tasks improves across successive model versions (Rathje et al., 2024) and with size within one model family (Ziems et al., 2024), but none have specifically assessed which psychometric properties improve with size.
text.formatted: Other studies have shown that performance on text classification tasks improves across successive model versions <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Rathje et al., 2024)</ref> and with size within one model family <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Ziems et al., 2024)</ref>, but none have specifically assessed which psychometric properties improve with size.

text.text: The review above leaves us with two questions: What does a single convergent correlation tell us about a language-model measure?
And what model should researchers with sensitive transcripts choose?
Both these questions can be answered by a single experiment that only varies the scoring model and assesses models on those properties for which a criterion correlation alone is not informative.
We conducted such an experiment for two measures, described below, using a range of open-weight models of varying size, and comparing them to commercial frontier models.

In Study 2, we used two additional questionnaires, one assessing a construct that is proximal to the target (the proximal neighbor, suicide recovery), and one that is more distal (the distal neighbor, life satisfaction), to test whether the models' scores reflect the target construct rather than a neighboring one.
We address four questions.
First, does convergent validity increase with model size, and does the relation replicate across constructs?
Second, if open-weight and frontier models' scores are similarly correlated with a questionnaire, do the models differ in calibration, scoring failures, and repeatability?
Third, if a model passes the convergent criterion, does it actually measure the construct it is named after, and does the answer change with model size?
The distal neighbor test addresses the question of whether a model's scores measure the construct at all.
The proximal neighbor test is a more challenging version of this test.
Finally, what should a validation report for an LLM-derived measure include?
In both studies, we transcribed and scored clinical interviews zero-shot and compared the scores to validated self-report criteria.
All aspects of the interviews, including the prompt formatting and criteria, were held constant across all model configurations (cells) tested (Table 1; Supplement S1).
text.formatted: All aspects of the interviews, including the prompt formatting and criteria, were held constant across all model configurations (cells) tested (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>; Supplement S1).

text.text: Among the open cells, only the scoring model differed; the frontier scores came from the provider's own software, with its own system prompt and sampling settings (Supplement S6.1).
We tested 52 model configurations across the two studies, as well as the extension study, and scored eight open cells (seven releases and one precision variant) in both studies.
Note.
Rows are grouped by developer; the text counts eight families (Gemma 3, Gemma 4, Granite 4, Llama 3.3, Ministral 3, Mistral, Qwen 3, Qwen 3.5).
Full specifications are in Supplement S1.
The nine models of the marketplace comparison are not counted (Supplement S6.2).

Models fall into two classes: open-weight models, which can be run on hardware controlled by the investigator, and frontier models, the reference class, which are the most powerful models currently available, and can only be accessed via an interface provided by the model vendor.
For open models, we measure model size in terms of the number of parameters actively used, since many model versions only activate a subset of their parameters for each query (Supplement S1).

This parameter count is confounded with other factors such as training data, architecture, pre-training date, and post-training alignment, but these are held relatively constant when comparing within a model family.

The corpus comprised 224 recovery-interview recordings from 150 participants, collected at three waves (𝑛 = 108,71, and 45 recordings) of a longitudinal cohort study examining recovery after a suicidal episode.
Participants were recruited online and screened in two stages (Supplement S3; Sokol et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Participants were recruited online and screened in two stages (Supplement S3; <ref type="bibr">Sokol et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: At each wave, they were asked to provide audio recordings of their responses to 15 standardized recovery prompts (average recording length = 33 minutes).
Recording was optional and was offered again at each wave, so 42 of the 150 participants made their first recording at the second or third wave.
The recordings were transcribed using Whisper (Radford et al., 2023), and sample selection, audio quality control, and transcript verification procedures are detailed in Sokol et al. (2026).
text.formatted: The recordings were transcribed using Whisper <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>, and sample selection, audio quality control, and transcript verification procedures are detailed in <ref type="bibr">Sokol et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: A single recording that was unscorable by all models was removed from validity analyses, but included in counts of scoring failures (224 requests per cell).
Participants consented to their de-identified transcripts being analyzed computationally and cloud-hosted (see Ethics Approval).

Validity, calibration, and repeatability analyses were conducted using data from the first recording of each participant (𝑛 = 149, after excluding one participant whose only recording was unscorable), of whom 74% reported at least one lifetime suicide attempt (demographics in Supplement S3).
text.formatted: Validity, calibration, and repeatability analyses were conducted using data from the first recording of each participant (𝑛 = 149, after excluding one participant whose only recording was unscorable), of whom 74% reported at least one lifetime suicide attempt (demographics in Supplement <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: The number of participants included was determined solely by the number of available recordings; no power calculation was performed.

The convergent criterion was the concurrent self-report total of the Recovery Evaluation and Suicide Support Tool (RESST), a 21-item, 1-5 measure of psychological suicide recovery based on the COURAGE model of recovery (Sokol et al., 2022) and validated in a recent study (Sokol et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The convergent criterion was the concurrent self-report total of the Recovery Evaluation and Suicide Support Tool (RESST), a 21-item, 1-5 measure of psychological suicide recovery based on the COURAGE model of recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Sokol et al., 2022)</ref> and validated in a recent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Sokol et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: All cells were given the recovery rubric (recovery_instructions_v3.txt) verbatim, without any example transcript or instructions for tuning the rubric to specific transcripts.
The rubric (Supplement S2.1) included anchored 1-5 scales for overall recovery, four subscales, and instructions to provide a final line with the five scores in JSON, a machine-readable format.
We kept the formatting identical across all cells, as models' performance can vary greatly with formatting (Sclar et al., 2023).
text.formatted: We kept the formatting identical across all cells, as models' performance can vary greatly with formatting <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Sclar et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The 30 open cells described in this work are 24 releases from seven families and six precision cells (Ministral 3 re-run at 8-bit and 16-bit precision; Supplement S6.3).
The size analyses described below are based on the 19 standard cells, which are 4-bit (Q4_K_M), instruction-tuned, and have at least 150 scorable transcripts.
The remaining 11 cells are each different in one aspect (see Supplement S1 for details).
text.formatted: The remaining 11 cells are each different in one aspect (see Supplement <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> for details).

text.text: The four Claude models of the instrument validation study (Sokol et al., 2026), used here as the frontier reference, were Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026a-d).
text.formatted: The four Claude models of the instrument validation study <ref type="bibr">(Sokol et al., 2026)</ref>, used here as the frontier reference, were Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 <ref type="bibr">(Anthropic, 2026a-d)</ref>.

text.text: We re-used the scores reported by these models, which were generated using Claude Code,
Anthropic's command-line tool (see Supplement S6.1 for details on the software used, which differs from that of the open cells).
Claude Code returns scores in a structured-output schema, rather than as parsed free text, and therefore frontier cells are not included in the audit of scoring failures.
Software All open models tested in both studies were run on a single cloud-hosted NVIDIA A100 using Ollama (versions, sampling settings, and truncation check in Supplement S6.1).
In addition, we tested uncontrolled software settings by scoring nine open models through commercial thirdparty hosts in a separate marketplace comparison (Supplement S6.2).
Study 2: Future Self-Continuity (FSC) Corpus and Replication Sample Data for Study 2 come from the sample of Sokol and Goodman (2026; scores publicly available at OSF: 10.17605/OSF.IO/JC86M).
The sample comprises 164 verbatim transcripts of open-ended interviews about the future self.
Participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and screened by CloudResearch (demographics in Supplement S4).
text.formatted: Participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and screened by CloudResearch (demographics in Supplement <ref type="figure">S4</ref>).

text.text: This sample is mixed-risk, with 19.5% reporting a lifetime suicide attempt and 56.7% reporting pastyear suicidal ideation (Sokol et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This sample is mixed-risk, with 19.5% reporting a lifetime suicide attempt and 56.7% reporting pastyear suicidal ideation <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sokol et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: All 164 transcripts were used in this study.
The convergent criterion was the total score on the Future Self-Continuity Questionnaire (FSCQ; Sokol & Serper, 2020).

The eight open cells were scored on the same A100 and software setup as Study 1 (Supplement S6.1).
The frontier group consisted of the six successive Claude versions released from June 2024 to July 2026 (scoring sources in Supplement S1; one excluded scoring pass in Supplement S5.3).
To test whether larger open models have better discriminant validity, we added an extension study on a local ASUS Ascent GX10 workstation (128 GB unified memory; ASUS, 2025; Supplement S7.1).
First, we re-scored Gemma 3 12B and 27B on the GX10 and compared them to the A100 on three bridge criteria (Supplement S7.1).

In advance, we set a rule that if any criterion was not met, cells from the GX10 would be reported separately and would not be pooled with A100 cells in any slope, group mean, or cross-study correlation.
We then scored two models.
Gemma 4 31B, the most valid open model of Study 1, was not scored in Study 2 because of computational constraints; it was scored here in two independent passes.
Llama 3.3 70B, the largest model that could be run on the workstation, was scored in a single pass (model tags in Supplement S7.1).
Convergent validity and model size.
Convergent validity was assessed by computing the Pearson correlation (𝑟) with the target criterion.
Where "validity" appears below without qualification, it refers to this coefficient.
We regressed Fisher 𝑧-transformed correlations on log 10 active parameters and computed model-level and participant-level bootstrap intervals (2,000 replicates; Efron & Tibshirani, 1994).

Agreement.

The difference between the target and neighbor correlations (𝑟 target -𝑟 neighbor ), the target and neighbor partial correlations (the model score's partial correlation with the target controlling for the neighbor, and with the neighbor controlling for the target), and Williams's (1959) 𝑡-test for dependent correlations that share the model score, were used as discriminant validity indices.
Even a measure of Construct A alone (a pure measure) will be correlated with a neighboring Construct B, because the two constructs share true variance.

Our goal was to answer two questions : (1) What does a single convergent correlation tell us about a language-model measure?
(2) What model should researchers with sensitive transcripts choose?
The answer to the second question appears straightforward based on the typical evidence presented in this field.

Convergent validity, as assessed by correlation with a criterion measure, clearly improves with model size, both across the open models and from the open models to the frontier models, whose sizes are not disclosed but are thought to be much larger.
In fact, in both studies, the standard open-weight models achieved, on average, roughly three-quarters of the frontier's convergent validity.
Thus, it appears that the decision comes down to cost.
However, a convergent-only approach does not capture any of the properties that differentiate a valid measure from an invalid one with the same or a similar correlation.

A more nuanced answer requires examining four further properties: whether the model distinguishes the target from neighboring constructs (discriminant validity), whether its scores agree with the scale in absolute terms (calibration), whether it produces a usable score for each case (scoring failures), and whether repeated scoring passes give consistent scores (repeatability).

Regarding discriminant validity, the standard open models (all models with ≤ 27B parameters) do not differentiate between future self-continuity and suicide recovery, whereas the frontier generations do.
Regarding calibration, in Study 1, the open and frontier models differed most in a correctable constant bias of up to a full scale point, which cannot be detected by 𝑟.
Regarding scoring failures, in the worst cell, the model provided no valid score for one-third of the sample.
Finally, regarding repeatability, smaller models provided less consistent scores across repeated passes and, after correction for that inconsistency, still scored less validly.

A convergent-only validation strategy, which focuses on the target alone, would have led researchers to conclude that all of the standard open models were valid, the error Campbell and Fiske (1959) warned against.
text.formatted: A convergent-only validation strategy, which focuses on the target alone, would have led researchers to conclude that all of the standard open models were valid, the error <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Campbell and Fiske (1959)</ref> warned against.

text.text: The problem is not that the models are all inaccurate in their scoring of the target, since they are all able to discriminate between future self-continuity and life satisfaction, at least in terms of direction.
The problem arose with the proximal neighbor, where these constructs are similar in that they both have narrative themes of future orientation, hope, and recovery.
There are three non-mutually exclusive interpretations of these results, all of which should be treated as exploratory.
First, the smaller models may be scoring a general impression of how well the person is doing, which is what both questionnaires are doing.
When controlling for recovery, the smaller models' association with the target was about half that of the frontier models.
Second, the failure may be specific to the facet that distinguishes the construct.
The open models were able to score positive affect toward the future self about as validly as the frontier models, but they scored similarity between present and future self poorly.

Their overall scores were strongly correlated with their Positivity scores, which is the subscale of future selfcontinuity most strongly related to recovery (FSCQ subscale correlations with the RESST:
Positive affect 𝑟 = .690, Similarity 𝑟 = .365; Supplement S5.4).

A composite score can therefore correlate well with its criterion while the model fails on the facet that separates the target from its neighbor, so facet scores can show why good convergent validity does or does not come with good discriminant validity.
Third, part of the failure may be due to characteristics of the material itself.
In a mixed-risk sample, the interviews contain recovery content that a less discriminating model may include in its rating.
However, the extension study changed this interpretation.
In fact, in our tests Gemma 4 31B fell within the observed frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, and its proximal difference did not differ significantly from the frontier mean.
What set Gemma 4 31B apart from other models was not its size alone.
Its predecessor, Gemma 3 27B, which is nearly as large, failed to distinguish the target from its proximal neighbor even on the same workstation.
Similarly, Llama 3.3 70B, more than twice as large as Gemma 4 31B, did not show greater discriminant validity.

Discriminant validity is possible in a locally run model, but in these data it depended on the release, not on parameter count alone, and it only emerged in the largest models that a single workstation can run.
The issue of absolute calibration is particularly relevant when scores are compared to a threshold, as opposed to when scores are ranked.
In Study 1, the open models were systematically higher than the frontier models, but their scatter was only modestly wider.
This pattern can be removed with a calibration subsample: participants who are scored by both the model and the questionnaire.
Since approximately half of the open cells showed proportional bias, a correction that accounts for both the intercept and the slope is necessary.
All models, including frontier generations, rated participants higher for future self-continuity than the questionnaire.
This bias is a property of the combination of rubric, interview, and questionnaire, and not of any particular model.
Calibration does not, however, correct poor discriminant validity.

A linear correction removes constant and proportional bias without changing the model's correlation with the target or with either neighbor, so a calibrated score can agree more closely with the questionnaire in absolute terms while still reflecting a broader or different construct.
Correcting for imperfect repeatability reduced the slope on model size by about a fifth (by an imprecise point estimate), but did not eliminate it.
This suggests that scores from a single pass underestimate the validity a small model can achieve.
Averaging repeated passes is an untested but inexpensive correction that can be used locally.
It should be emphasized that repeatability differs from the reliability of a human rater.
Rescoring reruns the same model in the same state, so repeatability reflects only the random variation in the model's own responses, which a lower temperature reduces.
High repeatability therefore shows that a model scores consistently, not that it measures the construct (Gemma 4 31B in Study 1: repeatability 𝑟 = .957, convergent 𝑟 = .661).
There are two important limitations on how these measures can be used.

First, none of the configurations examined here, including the frontier, were sufficiently similar to the questionnaire to allow them to be used as a replacement for the questionnaire for any individual.
Even the most valid models had approximately one in ten participants whose scores differed from their self-report by more than a full scale point.
Second, the frontier series demonstrates that researchers cannot depend on newer models to provide increased validity.
Over 25 months, six frontier generations of models were examined, and yet convergent validity of the selfcontinuity pairing remained largely unchanged.
Newer model generations may improve in certain capacities while not improving in the validity of their rubric scoring.
As new generations are released and general capacities improve, each needs to be reassessed for validity.

It is likely that future increases in validity will be found through careful psychometric design of subscales, structured elicitation, and calibration subsamples, rather than merely through adopting a newer model.
The cells that failed to score transcripts were the less valid ones; therefore, the presence of unscored cases did not inflate the reported validity of any model.
However, the risk is not just about individual cases.
If failures are concentrated on ambiguous or atypical transcripts, they will determine the analytic sample (Rubin, 1976).

text.text: In two cells, the participants that the model failed to score differed on the criterion from the ones it did score.
Researchers should note and inspect all first-attempt failures, rather than ignore them or re-score them without recording the failure.
Current standards in psychology require validity evidence for every intended interpretation of a score (AERA, APA, & NCME, 2014; see also Lin, 2026).

text.text: However, the field has not yet agreed on how this standard should be interpreted when the instrument under consideration combines a model, a rubric, and a software setup.
There are many opportunities for defensible choices in language-model measurement (model, precision, software setup, and prompt), and there are reporting standards for this kind of flexibility.
Box 1 outlines a minimum standard of five evidence domains: one for the convergent evidence the field already reports, and one for each property that convergent evidence cannot detect.
Within each domain, other analyses that answer the same question can replace those listed.

This standard is the psychometric counterpart of two existing reporting standards: REFORMS, for machine-learningbased science (Kapoor et al., 2024), and TRIPOD-LLM, for reporting the processing steps, sampling settings included (Gallifant et al., 2025).

text.text: However, neither tests discriminant validity or reports limits of agreement, both of which we view as essential.
The five domains in Box 1 are intended as a minimum for evaluating numerical scores derived from psychological interviews, rather than an exhaustive account of measurement quality.
Box 1.
Minimum validation evidence for an LLM-derived psychological measure 1.
Convergent validity.
Pearson and Spearman correlations with a validated criterion and, where possible, the same correlations for reference models scored on the same material.
Discriminant validity.

Correlations with concurrently administered neighboring instruments; the difference between the target and neighbor correlations (𝑟 target -𝑟 neighbor ), Williams's test for dependent correlations, target and neighbor partial correlations, and comparison with the values expected for a pure measure, adjusted for attenuation.
Bland-Altman agreement.
Mean bias, standard deviation of differences, 95% limits of agreement, the share of the mean squared difference due to constant bias, and a regression test for proportional bias.
Audit of first-attempt scoring failures.

All initial failures from raw logs, classed as format failures, truncations, or refusals; the analytic sample size per model configuration; and a test of whether missingness relates to participant characteristics.
Repeatability.
Consistency and absolute agreement (ICC(A,1)) across repeated independent scoring passes under operational settings, with validity reported both observed and disattenuated.
High repeatability shows that the model scores consistently, not that its scores are valid.

In this study, a 12B to 31B open-weight model was sufficient to achieve most of the frontier's convergent validity (65% to 96% of the frontier mean in Study 1), without the need for a third-party processor.
Through a commercial marketplace, it cost roughly one-fortieth of the estimated per-transcript cost of a frontier model at July 2026 prices (Supplement S6.5).
When used in conjunction with the other recommendations in Box 1, this model can provide a valuable research tool.

Models should be run on dedicated hardware with the model version, software version, context length, and temperature all fixed; when we ran open models through a commercial marketplace, the relation between model size and validity was eliminated.
When a measure must discriminate between a target and a proximal clinical neighbor, researchers should not assume that a standard open model will suffice.
In these data, the best-performing locally run configuration was Gemma 4 31B.

Whatever model is chosen, researchers should test the difference between the target and neighbor correlations for the construct being measured rather than infer discriminant validity from the model's size or recency.
Scores should be interpreted as absolute scores only after correction against a calibration subsample.

With about 50 participants, a calibration subsample gives a standard error of the mean difference of about 0.15 points on a 5point scale; where proportional bias is present, the slope must be estimated as well, which needs a larger subsample.
Investigators should check scoring failures on a subset of their sample before scoring the full sample.

In cases where quantization may be preferred for practical reasons, it is noteworthy that in our studies eight-bit precision produced no detectable loss of validity at any size tested, and any loss of validity when using 4-bit precision was limited to the smallest models tested.
Limitations This set of studies has six limitations.

(1) In comparing released models, we cannot isolate the effects of active parameter count from other factors that influence performance, such as training data (Hoffmann et al., 2022), architecture, and alignment.
Thus, cross-family comparisons should be interpreted as comparisons of releases, not families.
(2) Our sample of 52 configurations is a purposive sample of prominent releases, so the relations between model size and validity characterize these releases, not all LLMs.
Likewise, the open-versus-frontier comparisons concern the releases tested here, not two classes of models.
(3) We tested discriminant validity for a single construct pair in a single sample.
The open cells in Study 2 were not rescored, and therefore, their correlations are uncorrected for attenuation.
This means that while we demonstrate that failure can occur, we do not estimate its prevalence across clinical domains.
In addition, the questionnaires served as criteria, not as true scores.
A transcriptderived score may contain construct-relevant variance that a self-report questionnaire misses, so the validity estimated here is relative to these criteria and their expected relations.
(4) Our frontier reference was a model family from a single provider, scored with different software than the open cells.
(5) The extension study includes two models, one of which was scored in a single pass.
Its results should be treated as tentative until replicated.
We chose Gemma 4 31B as the most valid open model of Study 1 for use in the extension study.
This choice could have overstated its convergent validity (though not its discriminant validity). ( 6) Every cell in our study uses the same transcription.

text.text: A measure can pass a commonly used convergent-validity check while failing on properties essential to its intended interpretation.

Specifically, a model can correlate . 50 with its target questionnaire and just as strongly with a neighboring construct, increase or decrease each score by a scale point, not score certain types of cases, and give a different score on a second pass.
The use of a convergent correlation would not detect any of these issues.
This is not novel to psychometrics: Discriminating between a valid measure and an invalid measure with a similar correlation is standard practice that should be applied to our new LLM-based methods.
This is often not challenging.
Most of what is needed can be calculated from data that have already been collected, and the questionnaire needed for a discriminant test is often already part of the battery.
We hope that researchers will take these steps and report the five domains in Box 1 before adopting further automated measures.

1 Study 1: recovery rubric (recovery_instructions_v3.txt) <background> This assessment measures personal recovery following a suicidal episode, as d efined by the Recovery Evaluation and Suicide Support Tool (RESST; Sokol et a l., 2023).
text.formatted: 1 Study 1: recovery rubric (recovery_instructions_v3.txt) <background> This assessment measures personal recovery following a suicidal episode, as d efined by the Recovery Evaluation and Suicide Support Tool (RESST; Sokol et a l., 2023).

text.text: Personal recovery is distinct from clinical recovery: it does not require the remission of symptoms or the absence of distress.

Following Anthony (1993), it is "a way of living a satisfying, hopeful, and contributing life even with in the limitations caused by illness"-a deeply personal process of reclaiming agency, worth, connection, and meaning.
A person can therefore be well into recovery while still describing pain, struggle, and difficult circumstances.
You are scoring recovery-not symptom severity, suicide risk, likeability, or verbal fluency.
Distressing content, inarticulate speech, or morally admirabl e behavior are not, in themselves, evidence in either direction.
The transcript contains a participant's spoken answers to up to 15 open-ended prompts spanning the four domains below; some participants answered fewer th an 15.
The RESST conceptualizes suicide personal recovery as a single global constru ct composed of four interrelated lower-order domains.

Assess each domain on t he basis of what the transcript reveals about the person's current lived expe rience-both what they state explicitly and what is implicit in how they descr ibe themselves, their life, and their relationships: 1.
Self-Worth: A positive sense of self-identity.

The degree to which the per son likes and accepts themselves (even when others do not accept them), trust s themselves, feels confident handling life's challenges, has learned to thin k about themselves in a more positive way, is proud of who they are becoming, and is able to forgive themselves.
Life Worth: Meaning and the desire to live.
The degree to which the person experiences meaning and purpose, has something or someone worth living for, is willing to live, and feels that life is worth living even with its ups and downs.
Social Worth: Feeling accepted within meaningful relationships.
The degree to which the person feels cared about, safe, connected, accepted, valued, an d respected within mutually respectful relationships-a sense of belonging and mattering to others.
Assign a score between 1 and 5 for each subcomponent (Self-Worth, Life Wor th, Social Worth, and Self-Understanding) and for overall recovery.
Scores ma y include decimals (e.g., 3.5) to express placement between adjacent rubric a nchors.
Do not penalize a person for describing pain, struggle, or hard circumstan ces if they also convey genuine self-worth, meaning, connection, or self-unde rstanding.
Withdrawal from relationships framed as not needing others is evid ence of limited, not strong, Social Worth.

If the transcript contains ambiguous, incomplete, or contradictory informa tion, use your best judgment to interpret the overall sense conveyed, weighin g the person's prevailing current experience over isolated or past statements.

If the transcript contains too little construct-relevant content to score (for example, the participant declines to answer, the recording is essentiall y empty, or the content does not address any of the prompts), do not estimate scores.
Instead, state briefly why the transcript is unscoreable and output the insufficient-transcript JSON specified in the output format.
A short tran script that nonetheless contains substantive construct-relevant content shoul d be scored.

Transcripts are automatic speech-to-text and may contain disfluencies, tra nscription errors, the participant reading the interview prompts aloud, or oc casionally the same passage duplicated by a recording artifact.
Do not treat read-aloud prompt text as the participant's own narrative or count duplicated passages as additional evidence.
For each score, follow this process: a.
Review the transcript as it relates to the construct and rubric b.
Think step-by-step to develop an assessment c.
Provide the numerical assessment 8.
Use the rubrics provided below to guide your scoring.
</instructions> <rubrics> Self-Worth Rubric: 1: Self-worth absent or negative.
text.formatted: </instructions> <rubrics> Self-Worth Rubric: 1: Self-worth absent or negative.

text.text: Dislikes or distrusts self, cannot accept o r forgive self, and expresses no pride in who they are.
2: Largely lacking self-worth.
Little self-acceptance; struggles to trust or forgive self; self-view is mostly critical or contingent on others' approval.
3: Mixed or conditional self-regard.
Some self-acceptance, self-trust, confid ence, and pride, but fragile, uneven, or contingent; self-forgiveness is diff icult and inconsistent.
4: Generally positive self-regard.

Likes and accepts self (largely independen t of others' approval), trusts own judgment, feels confident handling challen ges, is usually able to forgive self, and takes pride in their growth, despit e some self-doubt.
5: Robust self-worth.
Consistently likes, accepts, and trusts self; feels con fident and capable; forgives self; is proud of who they are becoming; and mai ntains this regard even when others do not affirm it.
Life Worth Rubric: 1: Sees little or no meaning or purpose; few or no reasons for living; ambiva lent, indifferent, or negative about being alive.
2: Tenuous sense of meaning and few reasons for living, though willingness to live is present even if fragile or newly re-established.
3: Some meaning and reasons for living, but inconsistent or conditional; the sense that life is worth living coexists with significant doubt or difficulty.
4: Clear sources of meaning and purpose and identifiable reasons for living; affirms that life is worth living through its ups and downs.
5: Strong, stable sense of meaning and purpose; firm reasons for living; clea rly values life and conveys a sense of actively choosing it.

Social Worth Rubric (weight the overall felt sense of belonging across the pe rson's relationships; one secure relationship amid otherwise absent or hurtfu l relationships typically indicates the middle of the scale, not the top): 1: Feeling cared for, safe, connected, or valued is absent from the person's account; relationships are missing, hostile, or harmful.
2: Minimal connection; doubts that others genuinely care; limited safety or s ense of being valued in relationships.
3: Some genuine connection and care, but inconsistent, partial, or uncertain; mixed sense of being valued, safe, and respected.
4: Generally feels cared about, safe, connected, accepted, and valued within meaningful, mutually respectful relationships, despite some remaining strain, distance, or unevenness.
5: Strong, secure sense of belonging across relationships; consistently feels deeply cared for, safe, valued, and connected within mutually respectful rel ationships.
Self-Understanding Rubric: 1: Self-understanding absent; confused by own reactions; fragmented or unclea r sense of who they are.
2: Limited insight; often confused or surprised by own reactions; weak cohere nce in their sense of self.
3: Moderate insight; understands some aspects of self, reactions, and behavio rs; partial coherence; some integration of past experiences.
4: Good self-understanding; aware of own strengths, challenges, and character istic thought and emotional patterns; a fairly coherent sense of self; connec ts current challenges to life history.

5: Deep, integrated self-understanding; clear grasp of strengths, challenges, and inner reactions; a coherent identity narrative that meaningfully situate s current challenges within one's life history.

Overall Recovery Rubric (a holistic judgment across the four domains, typical ly near their average; a markedly low single domain should lower, but not dom inate, the overall score): 1: Little to no sense of personal recovery.
Worthlessness or emptiness, life feeling not worth living, disconnection or isolation, and little self-underst anding.
2: Minimal or fragile recovery.
Predominantly negative or depleted sense of s elf, tenuous reasons for living, weak or strained connection, and limited sel f-understanding.
3: Moderate, mixed recovery.
Ambivalent or conditional self-worth, a sense th at life is worth living that is qualified or effortful, some meaningful conne ction, and partial self-understanding.
4: Considerable recovery.
Generally positive sense of self, a clear sense tha t life is worth living, meaningful and supportive connection, and good self-u nderstanding, with some remaining struggles.

text.text: <background> Future self-continuity (FSC) refers to the psychological connectedness people have with their future selves-the sense of persistence of selfhood from the present to the future.
text.formatted: <background> Future self-continuity (FSC) refers to the psychological connectedness people have with their future selves-the sense of persistence of selfhood from the present to the future.

text.text: It represents the degree to which a person identifies their future self as being the same person as their current self.
FSC has three subcomponents: 1.
Similarity to the future self: How similar one's current self is to their future self in terms of beliefs, values, personality, and other aspects of id entity.
Vividness of the future self: How vividly an individual can imagine their future self and project themselves into the future.
Similarity to Future Self Rubric: 1: Expects very little similarity between current and future self.
2: Anticipates a few similarities in minor aspects, but expects core identity to change.
3: Expects moderate similarity, with some core aspects remaining consistent a nd others changing.
4: Envisions considerable similarity, with most key aspects of identity remai ning continuous.
5: Anticipates high similarity, with beliefs, values, personality and identit y largely unchanged.
6: Expects very high similarity bordering on sameness between current and fut ure self.
Vividness of Future Self Rubric: 1: Has little to no ability to imagine or envision the future self.
Future se ems abstract and unreal.
2: Can imagine the future self to a minimal degree, but the image is vague, h azy and lacks detail.
3: Has a moderately vivid image of the future self.
Can envision some details but much is still unclear.
4: Can envision the future self with considerable vividness and clarity.
Has a fairly detailed picture.
5: Has a highly vivid and clear mental image of the future self.
Can imagine many specific details.
6: Can picture the future self with extraordinary vividness and detail, almos t like a mental time travel.
Positivity Toward Future Self Rubric: 1: Has strongly negative feelings toward future self.
Actively dislikes or fe ars future self.
2: Feels somewhat negative toward future self.
Has doubts, concerns, and expe cts to dislike future self.
3: Has mixed or ambivalent feelings.
Feels somewhat positive and somewhat neg ative toward future self.
4: Feels largely positive toward future self.
Cares about, has good expectati ons and wants good for future self.
5: Has strongly positive affect toward future self, with feelings of liking, caring and warm regard.
6: Has extremely positive feelings toward future self, with deep fondness, co ncern and sense of kinship.

text.text: Study 1 recruitment.

Low et al. (2026), for example, proposed a broader framework for text psychometrics and demonstrated an additional test of content validity based on whether models detect expertidentified prototypical expressions of a construct.

text.text: Their approach tests whether the model captures the range of expressions associated with a construct, whereas our discriminant comparisons test whether a model's scores correlate more strongly with the target questionnaire than with neighboring ones.
Criterion performance alone does not establish either that a model captures the content of a construct or that its scores are specific to that construct.
Both forms of evidence are informative, but neither substitutes for the other.
Other properties, particularly fairness and generalizability across populations and interview settings, may require additional tests depending on the intended use.
